title: Lettres persanes
author: Montesquieu
blurb: Two Persian travellers write home about Paris: houses built in the air, a king who turns paper into money, cafés that make people witty, and a fashion that changes before a letter can arrive.

p: Usbek to his friend Rustan, in Isfahan.
We stayed only a day in Qom. After praying at the tomb of the Virgin, we set off again, and yesterday we arrived in Tabriz.
Rica and I are perhaps the first Persians whom the desire for knowledge has driven out of their country, and who have given up the comforts of a quiet life to go in search of wisdom.
We were born in a rich kingdom, but we did not believe that our knowledge had to stop at its borders.
Tell me what people think of our journey. Do not flatter me: I know very well that few people approve of it.
Address your letter to Erzurum, where I shall stay some time. Farewell, my dear Rustan. Be sure that wherever in the world I may be, you have a faithful friend.
From Tabriz, the 15th of the moon of Safar, 1711.
We have been in Paris for a month, and we have been constantly on the move.
Paris is as big as Isfahan. The houses are so tall that you would swear they were inhabited only by astrologers.
You can well imagine that a city built in the air, with six or seven houses on top of one another, is extremely crowded.
You may not believe it, but in the month I have been here, I have not yet seen anyone walk.
There are no people in the world who make better use of their legs than the French: they run, they fly.
I, who am not used to this pace, and who often go on foot without changing speed, sometimes get as furious as a Christian.
It's one thing to be splashed from head to foot; but I cannot forgive the elbow jabs I receive every day.
A man who comes up behind me and overtakes me turns me half round, and another who passes me the other way suddenly puts me back where the first had pulled me from.
The King of France is the most powerful prince in Europe. He has no gold mines like the King of Spain, but he has more wealth than him.
That is because he draws it from the vanity of his subjects, which is more inexhaustible than mines.
Besides, this king is a great magician: he wields his power over the very minds of his subjects; he makes them think as he wishes.
If he has only a million crowns in his treasury and needs two, he only has to persuade them that one crown is worth two, and they believe it.
If he has a difficult war to wage and has no money, he only has to put it into their heads that a piece of paper is money, and they are at once convinced.
What I tell you about this prince should not surprise you: there is another magician, stronger than he is, who is no less master of his mind than he himself is of others'.
This magician is called the Pope. Sometimes he makes the king believe that three are only one; at other times, that the bread one eats is not bread, or that the wine one drinks is not wine.
The inhabitants of Paris have a curiosity that verges on the extravagant.
When I arrived, people looked at me as if I had been sent from heaven: old men, men, women, children, everyone wanted to see me.
If I went out, everyone came to their windows; if I was in the Tuileries, I would immediately see a circle forming around me.
If I was at the theatre, I found a hundred opera glasses trained on my face. In short, never has a man been so much looked at as I was.
I sometimes smiled to hear people who had hardly ever left their rooms saying to one another: 'You have to admit he looks very Persian.'
So many honours could only become burdensome. I resolved to take off my Persian clothes and put on European ones, to see whether there would still be anything remarkable about my face.
This experiment taught me what I was really worth.
Free of all foreign ornaments, I found myself valued at my exact worth. I suddenly fell into a dreadful nothingness.
I would sometimes remain for an hour in company without anyone having looked at me.
But if someone, by chance, told the company that I was Persian, I would at once hear a murmur around me:
'Ah! Monsieur is Persian? What an extraordinary thing! How can anyone be Persian?'
Coffee is very much in use in Paris. There are a great many public houses where it is served.
In some of these houses, people exchange news; in others, they play chess.

There is one where the coffee is prepared in such a way that it gives wit to those who drink it: at least, of all those who come out, there is nobody who does not believe he has four times more of it than when he went in.
But what shocks me about these wits is that they do not make themselves useful to their country, and that they use their talents on childish things.
For example, when I arrived in Paris, I found them heated over the slightest dispute imaginable:
it concerned the reputation of an old Greek poet whose homeland and time of death have been unknown for two thousand years.
Both sides admitted he was an excellent poet; the only question was how much merit should be given to him.
Each wanted to set the rate; but among these distributors of reputation, some gave better measure than others. That was the quarrel!
I find the whims of fashion among the French astonishing.
They have forgotten how they were dressed this summer; they have even less idea how they will be dressed this winter.
But above all, you would not believe how much it costs a husband to keep his wife in fashion.

What use would it be to give you an exact description of their clothes and ornaments? A new fashion would come and destroy all my work, and before you had received my letter, everything would have changed.
A woman who leaves Paris to spend six months in the country comes back as old-fashioned as if she had been forgotten there for thirty years.
The son does not recognise his mother's portrait, so foreign does the dress she is painted in seem to him.
Sometimes hairstyles rise little by little, and a revolution brings them down all at once.
There was a time when their immense height put a woman's face in the middle of her own person; at another, it was her feet that occupied that place.

Architects have often been obliged to raise, lower and widen their doors, according to whether women's finery demanded this change of them, and the rules of their art have been made slaves to these whims.
The other day I was in a company where I saw a man very pleased with himself.
In a quarter of an hour, he settled three questions of morals, four historical problems and five points of physics.
I have never seen such a universal decider: his mind was never held up by the slightest doubt.
We left the sciences; we talked about the news of the day: he passed judgement on the news of the day.
I wanted to catch him out, and I said to myself: 'I must get onto my own ground; I'll take refuge in my country.'
I spoke to him about Persia. But hardly had I said four words to him than he contradicted me twice, on the authority of two travellers.
'Good heavens!' I said to myself, 'what sort of man is this? Soon he'll know the streets of Isfahan better than I do!'
My mind was soon made up: I fell silent, I let him talk, and he is still deciding.
I see people here who argue endlessly about religion, but it seems that at the same time they are competing to see who will practise it least.
These people are not better Christians, nor even better citizens, and that is what troubles me.
For, whatever religion one lives in, observing the laws, love for one's fellow men and devotion to one's parents are always the first acts of religion.
Indeed, should not the first aim of a religious man be to please the Divinity that established the religion he professes?
Now, the surest way to achieve this is no doubt to observe the rules of society and the duties of humanity.
For, whatever religion one has, as soon as one supposes one, one must also suppose that God loves people, since he establishes a religion to make them happy.
The best way to please him is therefore to make others happy, and to fulfil towards them the duties of justice.
During all these years, Usbek ruled from afar his household in Isfahan, where his wives lived shut away, guarded by servants who obeyed him.
He wrote about freedom and justice; but at home, he knew nothing but authority.
One day, he receives a last letter. It is from Roxane, the one among his wives he believed the most faithful.
Yes, I deceived you. I disobeyed your orders, and I managed to turn your dreadful seraglio into a place of delight and pleasure.
How could you think I was credulous enough to imagine that I was in the world only to worship your whims?
That, while you allow yourself everything, you had the right to crush all my desires?
No: I may have lived in servitude, but I have always been free.
I reformed your laws according to those of nature, and my mind has always remained independent.
You were astonished not to find in me the raptures of love. If you had really known me, you would have found all the violence of hatred.
When you receive this letter, I will no longer be there to answer you.
From the seraglio of Isfahan, the 8th of the moon of Rebiab I, 1720.

agissait: was about (il s'agissait de = it concerned)
aient: have (sans qu'ils aient besoin = without their needing)
air: look, air (avoir l'air = to look, seem)
ait: has (que le désir … ait fait = that desire has made)
arrêter: to stop (s'arrêter à = to stop at)
attraper: to catch (attraper froid = to catch cold)
au: to the, at the, in the
aurais: would have (j'aurais avoué = I would have confessed)
celui: the one (celui que = the one that)
cher: dearly (coûter cher = to cost a lot)
chez: at the home of (chez eux = at their place)
comme: like, as; how (comme c'est… ! = how … it is!)
content: pleased (content de lui = pleased with himself)
croie: believes (personne qui ne croie = nobody who doesn't believe)
demi-tour: half-turn (me fait faire un demi-tour = turns me half round)
dis-je: I said (dis-je en moi-même = I said to myself)
droit: right (avoir le droit de = to have the right to)
dès: from (dès le premier jour = from the very first day)
décisionnaire: someone who pronounces on everything (Montesquieu's coinage)
européenne: European (à l'européenne = in the European style)
eus-je: had I (à peine lui eus-je dit = hardly had I said)
eusses: had (avant que tu eusses reçu = before you had received)
eût: had (sans qu'on m'eût regardé = without anyone having looked at me)
fallait: was necessary (il fallait que = had to)
fort: strong; strong point (dans mon fort = on my own ground)
fusse: was (que je fusse = that I was)
joue: plays (on joue aux échecs = people play chess)
laissa: let (se laissa marier = let herself be married)
maison: home, house (à la maison = at home)
maître: master (maître de moi = my own master)
mette: put on (que je mette = that I put on)
nombre: number (un grand nombre de = a great many)
nouvelles: news (dire des nouvelles = to exchange news)
par: by, on (par terre = on the ground)
parti: side; decision (mon parti fut pris = my mind was made up)
parvenir: to achieve (y parvenir = to achieve it)
passe: (passe encore que = it's one thing that)
permets: allow (tu te permets tout = you allow yourself everything)
place: place (à sa place = in its place)
plus: more; no longer (ne … plus); most (le plus)
point: not at all (ne … point, literary 'pas'); point
pris: taken (mon parti fut pris = my mind was made up)
puisse: can (qu'il se puisse imaginer = that one could imagine)
quart: quarter (un quart d'heure = a quarter of an hour)
question: question

quitter: to take off, to part with
rendent: make themselves (se rendre utile = to make oneself useful)
saphar: Safar (a month of the Islamic calendar)
semble: seems (il me semble = it seems to me)
servirait: would serve (que me servirait de = what use would it be to)
sois: be (sois sûr = be sure); am (où je sois = wherever I may be)
su: known (je ne l'ai jamais su = I never found out)
tirent: make (tirer parti de = to make use of)
train: pace (fait à ce train = used to this pace)
trouve: find (pour qu'on ne le trouve pas = so that it wouldn't be found)
unes: ones (les unes sur les autres = on top of one another)
uns: some (les uns … les autres = some … others)
vis: saw (je me vis = I found myself)
vive: lives (quelque religion qu'on vive = whatever religion one lives in)
voilà: here is; (voilà dix ans que = for ten years now)
